reading.body:
Cloud AI services are dominated by US vendors, with eight of nine entries headquartered in the United States, Canada, or Israel, meaning the compute infrastructure underlying these APIs is concentrated in a small number of regulatory and geographic zones.

The pattern across these offerings is convergence on enterprise controls: data residency, identity integration, content filtering, and governance tooling appear repeatedly, across vendors that otherwise compete on model quality and price. That convergence reflects a real constraint. Enterprises deploying AI at scale need assurances about where data travels and who can audit model behavior, and cloud providers have built those controls directly into the API layer rather than leaving them to customers. IBM watsonx names hallucination detection and agent inventory explicitly; AWS Bedrock adds VPC support and model evaluation; Azure OpenAI Service specifies data residency controls. The feature lists are converging because the enterprise requirements are.

NVIDIA's presence as an inference microservices provider, rather than a hyperscaler, is the structural outlier here. It sits one layer below the others, closer to the GPU hardware, and its self-hosted option points to a different deployment model where the buyer controls the physical compute rather than renting it. The data does not cover pricing, latency, or actual model performance, so no comparison across vendors on those dimensions is possible. It also does not cover the power draw or data center footprint behind any of these services, which is the layer where capacity constraints actually bind.
